# SK2134 — Instance code writes to its own type's static field

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An instance constructor, method or accessor assigns a static field of its own type, so the last instance to run the line wins for every other instance and every thread.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2696, S3010 |

## Why

The write reads as per-instance initialization and is not. There is one slot: two objects that were meant to carry different values carry the same one, and two threads that construct at the same time lose an update between them. ⚠ **It survives review because the line is short and looks local** — `count++` in a constructor is four characters that describe a per-object act and perform a process-wide one — and it survives testing because a test that constructs one object never sees it.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    static Session? current;

    public Session(string user) {
        current = this;      // every session overwrites the last
        User = user;
    }

    public string User { get; }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    [ThreadStatic] static Session? current;

    Session(string user) => User = user;

    public static Session Begin(string user) => current = new Session(user);

    public string User { get; }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`CA2211` is a different question, and it was verified to be rather than assumed.** A probe at `AnalysisMode=All` reports `CA2211` on a `public static` field and says nothing about a `private static` one: it is about a field's *visibility*, it lands on the declaration, and it is silent about who writes it. This rule never reads visibility and never reports a declaration — it reports the write. The two overlap on exactly one shape, a public static field written from instance code, and there they say two different true things about it. ⚠ **Lazy initialization is the look-alike, and it is declined by recognising the guard rather than the name.** `_instance ??= new()` is instance code writing static state on purpose: the guard is what makes it write-once, so "the last one wins" is not true of it. A `??=`, an `x ?? y` right-hand side, and an assignment under an `if`, `while` or conditional whose condition mentions that same field together with `null` or `default` are all declined — the last form is what covers double-checked locking, where the inner test is the one the walk finds. The guard test is deliberately loose, because every shape it recognises produces silence and none of them can produce a finding. ⚠ **Only the enclosing type's own static fields.** `Console.Out = …` and `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture = …` are process-wide settings being set deliberately, usually once, by code that knows it; they are a different concept with a different answer, and admitting them would have made the exclusion list carry the rule. A `[ThreadStatic]` field is declined: it is one slot per thread and the sharing the finding complains about is not there. ⚠ **A write inside a lambda or a local function is declined**, because where it runs is not where it is written — a delegate handed to a scheduler is no longer instance code in the sense the finding means. `Interlocked.Increment(ref total)` is declined by construction rather than by a filter: it is an argument, not an assignment, so no assignment node exists for the rule to visit. ⚠ **A counter incremented from a constructor is reported, and that is intended rather than an oversight** — it is the canonical shape of this concept, it is not atomic, and the fixtures pin it positive so that nobody later mistakes it for a false positive and adds an exclusion. Report-only: making the state per-instance and making the member static change the type in opposite directions, and the assignment does not say which was meant. Generated code is excluded.
